title: The Prejudices of Mr. Market | Sanjay Bakshi | Talks at Google
description:
About the Talk:
Sanjay Bakshi’s talk will deal with select prejudices of Mr. Market in pricing of moated businesses. Illustrating each specific prejudice with an example, Sanjay will show how the stock market is deeply prejudiced in pricing moated businesses and that exploiting those prejudices - especially when they combine - has helped him in his investing process.

About the Author
Sanjay Bakshi is Adjunct Professor at Management Development Institute, Gurgaon, where he teaches MBA students a popular course titled “Behavioral Finance & Business Valuation (BFBV)”. He is also the author of the blog "Fundoo Professor" (https://fundooprofessor.wordpress.com ), where has written extensively about identifying durable competitive advantages in a business, and investment psychology. Sanjay is also the Managing Partner at ValueQuest Capital LLP.
summary: The speaker argues that value investors should utilize empathy as a key tool to understand the perspectives of customers, competitors, entrepreneurs, and Mr. Market. He emphasizes that while Mr. Market is an irrational, semi-psychotic creature driven by emotions, value investors must ignore his influence and instead take advantage of his prejudices when he acts foolishly.

transcript: MALE SPEAKER: Welcome, everyone, to our next episode of value investing talks in our series on investing. We have a very, very special guest with us today. He's traveled all the way from New Delhi, where he's a professor-- an adjunct professor-- at MDI. He teaches a very popular course to the MBA students over there which is titled Behavioral Finance and Business Valuation. He also blogs at Fundoo Professor and I've really enjoyed reading some of his articles there. So the nice thing about Sunday is that he's not only a teacher, he's also a practitioner. So in investing, it's very interesting when teaching and practice meet. And we are really looking forward to learning from your insights having worn both those hats. And he's one of the few who eats his own cooking and teaching as you could say. So without any further ado, ladies and gentlemen, please join me in welcoming Sanjay Bakshi. [APPLAUSE] SANJAY BAKSHI: Thank you, Sarab for inviting me here. It's a pleasure to be here. It's a wonderful campus and I'm delighted to be here with you today. My talk is titled "The Prejudices of Mr. Market." But I would like to talk to you, first, about and an unusual subject called empathy, which is the ability to step into the shoes of another person aiming to understand his or her feelings and perspectives, and to use that understanding to guide our actions. Empathy-- normally you don't associate this word with the world of capitalism and investing. And I have to admit that I used to take the same way too when I started out as a value investor about 21 years ago. But today I think differently. Today I think that every value investor should count empathy as one of the key tools in his or her toolkit. Today I use empathy to really understand a business and its market valuation. Let me explain how. I'm a value investor who focuses on investing in moated businesses in public markets in India. A moat, as you know, is a metaphor that Warren Buffett uses to illustrate the idea of a competitive advantage. And in one of his various talks, he said that what we're really trying to find is a business that, for one reason or another, has this moat around it. And you throw crocodiles and sharks and piranhas in the moat to make it harder and harder for people to swim across and attack the castle. So it's a very powerful metaphor. It's quite obvious to me that investing in a business with a moat carries a very low risk of permanent loss of capital. A durable competitive advantage makes a business resilient to economic shocks as well as managerial mistakes. It gives the business what Tom Russo, a wonderful investor who I'm told is going to be here and address you soon, likes to call this capacity to suffer. My own experience of more than two decades of value investing has persuaded me that investing in a business with a moat is likely to deliver much higher returns with much lower risk of permanent loss of capital than investing in a business without a moat. I am also convinced that buying into scalable businesses with moats at sensible prices and then holding onto them for long periods of time is a very profitable, low-stress investment strategy. But what about empathy? How do we use it for analyzing moated businesses? Well, while evaluating a business for a potential investor, I try to empathize with four types of people. I try to step into their shoes with an aim to understand their feelings and perspectives and to use their understanding to guide my firm's actions. Who are these people? Well, they're on the screen here. The first one, obviously, is the customer. I think it's terribly important to understand well about the pain of the customer that a business alleviates. Why does she prefer to buy from the company that you're evaluating? What's so special about the value proposition to customers that will make them want to come back again and again? The second one is the competitor. Why would a particular competitor not enter this market? You really have to put yourself in the shoes of a competitor and try to enter the market and see what will happen. So there are two kinds of situations that I have encountered in a moated situation-- one, that there is a moat, and people are going to try to enter, and they're going to get hurt, and they're not going to try again. And the second one is that they can't enter because of some regulatory reasons-- there is a patent, for example, or there is a regulatory monopoly. What are the entry barriers? Essentially, this is all about entry barriers. And I'm sure you're all very familiar with all of that. Put yourself in the shoes of a potential competitor. That's what it's all about. The third person is the entrepreneur. What drives the entrepreneur? Is he what Charlie Munger calls an intelligent fanatic? What struggles did he face in making this business a success? What would he do during tough times? What are his shortcomings? Are they so strong that you will reject partnering with him? Why? And finally, Mr. Market, why is the stock market misunderstanding this business? What are its prejudices? What will make them go away? For the rest of this talk, I will focus on the fourth person, Mr. Market. The first three are very obvious. I think you all know them very well. Anybody who has studied Porter knows about that. But the fourth person, Mr. Market, I think it's something worth knowing more about. Many years ago Warren Buffett called the stock market the semi-psychotic creature given to extremes of elation and despair. He was referring to the idea that markets are sometimes very inefficient in pricing assets. In his classic book "The Intelligent Investor," Ben Graham uses the metaphor of Mr. Market, which Warren Buffett has written and spoken about many times. And I quote, "Ben Graham, my friend and teacher, long ago described the mental attitude towards market fluctuations. And I believe to be the most conducive to investment success. He said that you should imagine market quotations coming from a remarkably accommodating fellow named Mr. Market who is your partner in a private business. Without fail, Mr. Market appears daily and names a price at which he will either buy your interest or sell you his. Even though the business that the two of you own may have economic characteristics that are stable, Mr. Market's quotations will be anything but, for, sad to say, the poor fellow has incurable emotional problems." "At times he feels euphoric and can see only favorable factors affecting the business. When in that mood, he names a very high buy/sell price because he fears that you may snap up his interest and rob him of imminent gains. At other times he's depressed and can see nothing but trouble ahead for both the business and the world. On those occasions he will name a very low price since he's terrified that you will unload your interest onto him." "Mr. Market has another endearing characteristic. He doesn't mind being ignored. If his quotation is uninteresting to you today, he'll be back with a new one tomorrow. Transactions are strictly at your option. Under these conditions, the more manic depressive his behavior, the better for you." "But like Cinderella at the ball, you must heed one warning or everything will turn into pumpkin and mice. Mr. Market is there to serve you and not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful. If he shows up some day in a particularly foolish mood, you're free to either ignore him or take advantage of him. But it'll be disastrous if you were to fall under his influence." I think every potential value investor or value investing student has read this many times. So it appears that Mr. Market really is what Warren Buffett has called "a semi-psychotic creature given to extremes of elation and despair." Yes, he is utterly irrational sometimes. And whenever that happens, value investors are going to take advantage of his prejudices. But here's the thing-- if Mr. Market is irrational and stays that way, then how will value investors make any money? For them to make money, Mr. Market should misprice assets only temporarily. And that is exactly what Ben Graham meant when he said that "in the short run, the market is a voting machine reflecting a voter registration test that requires only money, not intelligence or emotional stability. But in the long run, the market is like a weighing machine." Therein lies our opportunity. Once we know, one, that the stock market has a tendency of becoming extremely prejudiced against some business which, in our view, is exceptionally good, two, such prejudices produce very attractive market valuations for that business, and three, the market, however, tends in tendency of correcting its prejudice over time, we can really understand how to make intelligent investments. If we can understand why the market is prejudiced against a business we love and what will make those prejudices go away, then we'll have a basis for betting against the market. That is exactly what Seth Klarman meant when he wrote about the idea of necessary arrogance. He said that "at the root of value investing is the belief, first espoused by Ben Graham, that the market is a voting machine and not a weighing machine. Thus an investor must have more confidence in his or her own opinion than in the combined weight of all other opinions. This borders on arrogance, the necessary arrogance that is required to make investment decisions." "This arrogance must be tempered with extreme caution giving due respect to the opinions of others, many of whom are very intelligent and hard-working. Their sale of shares to you at seeming bargain prices may be the result of ignorance, emotion, or various institutional constraints. Or it may be that the apparent bargain is, in fact, flawed, that it is actually fairly priced or even overvalued and that sellers know more than you do." "This is a serious risk, but one that can be mitigated, first, by extensive fundamental analysis, and second, by knowing not only that something is bargain priced but, as best as you can, also why it is so. You never know for certain why sellers are getting out, but you may be able to reasonably surmise a rationale." I think Klarman has made a very important point here about the need to know the prejudices of Mr. Market. And many of those prejudices arise out of a shortcut called a representativeness heuristic, which means that we look for similar past experiences to make judgments about the probability of future events. So for example, if you run an insurance operation, you would have vast amounts of customer data that allows you to determine future likely behavior of a potential buyer of insurance. You would determine that probability and accordingly determine the insurance quotation based on categories. You will create these categories in your database. A potential buyer of insurance might, in your judgment, belong to a high risk category because he's a male, 20-year-old, young, alcohol-consuming, college-going student who has never owned a car before. For such a buyer, your quotation for selling car insurance would be higher than that of a low-risk category individual comprising of, say, a 35-year-old woman, a mother of two children who has never had an accident in her 10 years of car driving experience. Such type of categorization or stereotyping is essential for making quick judgments in any domain. Indeed, the very word "stereotyping" has an unnecessary negative connotation. In Daniel Kahneman's book, "Thinking, Fast and Slow," he writes, "'Stereotyping' is a bad word in our culture, but in my usage it is neutral. One of the basic characteristics of System 1 is that it represents categories as norms and prototypical exemplars." "This is how we think of horses, refrigerators, and New York police officers. We hold in memory a representation of one or more normal members of each of these categories. When the categories are social, these representations are called stereotypes." "Some stereotypes are perniciously wrong and hostile stereotyping can have dreadful consequences. But psychological facts cannot be avoided. Stereotypes, both correct and false, are how we think of categories." When Kahneman writes that some stereotypes are perniciously wrong, he's referring to such stereotyping as a key source of prejudice. In his wonderful book, "Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)," the psychologist Elliot Aronson writes, "Prejudices emerge from the disposition of the human mind to perceive and process information in categories. Categories is a nicer, more neutral word than stereotypes, but it is the same thing. Stereotypes are energy-saving devices that allow us to make efficient decisions on the basis of past experience, help us quickly process new information and retrieve memories, make sense of real differences between groups, and predict, often with considerable accuracy, how others will behave or how they think. We wisely rely on stereotypes and the quick information they give us to avoid danger, approach possible new friends, choose one school or job over another, or decide that the person across the crowded room will be the love of our lives." But when Kahneman also writes that hostile stereotyping can have dreadful consequences, he is really referring to sensitive social contexts such as hiring and racial profiling by, say, immigration authorities. He's not referring to the world of investing. In the world of investing, hostile stereotyping by Mr. Market can have wonderful consequences for the value investors. Take the case of the airline industry. Anyone who has read Warren Buffett's letters or watched his interviews on the subject knows just how bad the economics of the airline industry are. WARREN BUFFET: Yeah. MALE SPEAKER: Mr. Buffett, what prompted you to make an investment in US Air given the fact that this is such a cutthroat industry and certainly not transparent and easily understandable? WARREN BUFFET: Well, I think that, probably, the best answer is temporary insanity. [LAUGHTER] The fellow that runs US Air is a wonderful guy, but he just happens to be in an extraordinarily tough business. And the interesting thing is I had actually written something for Graham's book, in the early '70s, about how the airline business was about the toughest business there was. And the interesting thing of your question is that if you'd go back to the time-- and we're in the right state for that-- if we go back to the time of Kitty Hawk, net, the airline transport business in the United States has made no money. I mean, just think if you'd been down there in Kitty Hawk and you'd seen this guy go up. And all of a sudden this vision hits you that tens of millions of people would be doing this all over the world some day and it would bring us all closer together and everything. And you'd think, my god, this is something to be in on. And despite putting in billions and billions and billions of dollars, the net return to owners from being in the entire airline industry-- if you'd owned it all and you'd put up all this money-- is less than zero. If there had been a capitalist down there, the guy should have shot down Wilbur, you know what I mean? One small step for mankind and one huge step backwards for capitalism. But anyway, so along comes 1989 and I've got a lot of cash. And no one misled me in any way, shape or form. This is 100% my decision. And I put money in it. And Seth Schofield-- you can't find a better human being or manager than Seth Schofield. But he is operating with revenues based on market factors and costs that are not based on market factors. And that's a recipe for a lot of trouble. So I now have this-- SANJAY BAKSHI: I'll pause there, for the video. WARREN BUFFET: --800 number. And if I ever get the urge to buy an airline stock-- SANJAY BAKSHI: Buffett is obviously talking about the insensitivity towards base rates. WARREN BUFFET: --I dial this number. And I say, my name is Warren and I'm an "airoholic." And then this guy talks me down on the other end. SANJAY BAKSHI: He is telling us that before we invest in the airline industry, we should be aware that the odds of making money in that industry are bleak. That's because the overall economics of the airline industry suck. But that does not have to mean that we put every airline in the crappy business category in our mind. If we do that, then we will never invest in a Ryanair or a Southwest Airline, both of which are solid businesses which have beaten market indices handsomely over the last several years. Perhaps the analyst who did invest in either of these two businesses thought differently from the market without falling for the prejudice of applying the crappy business label to them. Perhaps she dug deeper and found that both businesses had durable competitive advantages and were run by entrepreneurs whom Charlie Munger would call intelligent fanatics. Perhaps she had reliable and persuasive evidence specific to those businesses which would go against the conclusion in the base rate that airlines are crappy businesses. Perhaps they were exceptional businesses which defied the rule. Perhaps she had the necessary arrogance based on the fact that she was right and Mr. Market was wrong. Exactly this type of thinking produces exceptional returns. When Mr. Market is deeply prejudiced against what you know to be a wonderful business, that very prejudice creates a fabulous investment opportunity. And so let's empathize with Mr. Market and understand its prejudices in the pricing of moated businesses. But before I do that I want to say some words of caution. First, these are the prejudice that I have found and exploited over the years, which means that there may be others which I have not found yet. Second, I only to prejudices in the pricing of moated businesses. To be sure, there are many other ways of practicing value investing. And the other kinds of value investing may result in your exploiting opportunities, prejudices which are very different from the one which I'm going to site right now. Finally, there will be overlaps in the sense that, sometimes, you will find multiple prejudices in a single situation. And when that happens, you can expect what Charlie Munger calls a lollapalooza outcome. My first prejudice is titled "Marshmallows." Here I want to talk about the tendency of investors to categorize stocks of businesses as cheap or expensive based on their reported P/E multiples. For example, many of my own value investing friends wouldn't want to buy into a business selling at a P/E multiple of 25. That's a prejudice in my view for two big reasons. First, there's plenty of evidence which disconfirms the notion that business selling at P/E multiples of 25 or above are expensive. By definition, a business that's expensive, if purchased at that expensive price, should deliver poor investment returns over the long term. But there's plenty of research which shows that's not the case. While the average business may well be overpriced at 25x, that doesn't mean that exceptional ones are also expensive at that market valuation. Charlie Munger's observation that "if a business earns 18% on capital over 20 or 30 years, even if you pay an expensive looking price, you'll end up with one hell of a result" is obviously applicable over here. And the second reason is that, in a moated business, reported earnings often understate true economic earnings. That's because money spent on successful moat expansion activities is charged off to P&L. But it should be treated as an expenditure with benefit spanning more than a year. This is a key point that Buffett has made in his letters and which, in my view, is often not fully understood by investors. Charlie Munger's observation that almost all good businesses engage in paying today, gain tomorrow activities also means that after making the necessary adjustments, one would find that the multiple of their economic earnings-- the ones that really matter-- are sometimes significantly lower than P/E multiples based on reported earnings. And so what looks optically expensive is really not that expensive. In my view, the market's tendency to categorize a business as expensive simply because it's trading at a 25 multiple is an inexplicable prejudice. Warren Buffett agrees. He wrote, many years ago, that the term "value investing" typically connotes the "purchase of stocks having attributes such as low ratio of price to book value, price to earnings ratio at a high dividend yield." Unfortunately, such characteristics, even if they appear in combination, are far from determinative as to whether an investor is indeed buying something for what it is worth and is therefore truly operating on the principles for obtaining value in his investments. Correspondingly opposite characteristics-- a high ratio of price to book value, a high price/earnings ratio, and a low dividend yield-- are in now way inconsistent with a value purchase. At this point you must be wondering, why did I title this part of the talk as "marshmallows." The answer to that question lies in a famous experiment which I'm sure many of you have heard of, the famous marshmallow experiment conducted in the neighborhood in Stanford University. This experiment is beautifully described in this video. JOACHIM DE POSADA: I'm here because I have a very important message. I think we have found the most important factor for success. And it was found close to here, at Stanford. A psychology professor took kids that were four years old and put them in a room all by themselves. And he would tell the child, a four-year-old kid, Johnny, I want to leave you here with a marshmallow for 15 minutes. If, after I come back, this marshmallow is here, you will get another one. So you will have two. To tell a four-year-old kid to wait 15 minutes for something that they like is equivalent to telling us, we'll bring you coffee in two hours, exactly equivalent. So what happened when the professor left the room? As soon as the door closed-- [SWISH]-- two out of three ate the marshmallow. Five seconds, 10 seconds, 40 seconds, 50 seconds, two minutes, four minutes, eight minutes-- some lasted 14.5 minutes-- [SWISH] [CHOMP]-- couldn't do it, could not wait. What's interesting is that one out of three would look at the marshmallow and go like this. Would look at it, put it back. They would walk around. They would play with their skirts and pants. That child already, at four, understood the most important principle for success, which is the ability to delay gratification, self-discipline, the most important factor for success. 15 years later-- 14, 15 years later-- follow-up study. What did they find? They went to look for these kids who were now 18 and 19. And they found that 100% of the children that had not eaten the marshmallow were successful. They have good grades. They were doing wonderful. They were happy. They had their plans. They have good relationships with the teachers, students. They were doing fine. A great percentage of the kids that ate the marshmallow, there were in trouble. They did not make it to the university. They have bad grades. Some of them dropped out. A few were still-- SANJAY BAKSHI: Why did most kids not wait? Two out of three kids didn't wait. Well, if you think about it, they were implicitly using DCF, discounted cash flow, to make their choice. The kid who could not wait for 15 minutes for another marshmallow was implicitly, at the subconscious level, using a very high discount rate to determine the present value of the second marshmallow. To her, two marshmallows 15 minutes later were not worth as much as one marshmallow now. And the only way that can happen is if she was using a very high discount rate. If kids can be myopic and over-weigh instant gratification and under-weigh delayed gratification, why not Mr. Market? Indeed, Buffett offers clues as to how he thinks about discount rates for valuing a business. He says, "When we look at the future of a business, we look at riskiness as a sort of go/no-go valve. In other words, if we think that we simply don't know what's going to happen in the future, that doesn't mean it's risky for everyone. It means we don't know and it's risky for us." "It may not be risky for someone else who understand the business. However, in this case, we just give up. We don't try to predict those things. We don't say, well, we don't know what's going to happen. Therefore we'll discount the cash flows that we don't know at 9% instead of 7%. That's not a good way to approach it." This is very fundamental. Because what he's saying is that in order to value a financial asset, he uses the same discount rate. He doesn't use the idea of equity risk premium at all. Clearly, Buffett does not use an equity risk premium in the discount rate. He does not heavily discount distant cash flows, delayed gratification, like the children in the marshmallow experiment. And that gives him an edge over competition, because he can pay up for quality. He's not actually overpaying for it. The second prejudice I'll call hidden champions. This is taken from a wonderful book called "Hidden Champions." in this book, the author writes about extremely successful businesses that have been below the radar for long periods of time, hidden champions, really. "Large corporations," he writes, "are the subject of close and constant scrutiny by academic researchers, analysts, shareholders, and journalists. Hidden champions, on the other hand, remain a virtually unexplored source of knowledge." Scattered about the globe, thousands of these highly successful companies are concealed behind a curtain of inconspicuous invisibility and, in some cases, deliberate secrecy." "This applies to the products these companies make and how they beat their competition. And even more difficult to research is how they're managed internally. Even their names are known to only a handful of experts, consultants, journalists, and researchers. This secretiveness contrasts starkly with the dominant positions the hidden champions enjoy in their markets." "Many of them have global market shares of more than 50% and even hold shares in the relevant market of 70% to 90%. On average, they're more than twice the size of their strongest competitors. Only a few large multinationals achieve comparable market positions." The question that he asks, I think, is very important. Why does this happen? Why do these outstanding companies remain below the radar? He offers many reasons, but the most obvious one is that the large number of the products offered by hidden champions go unnoticed by consumers. "Many of these companies operate in the hinterland of the value chain supplying machinery components or processes that are no longer discernible in the final product or service. As a result, the products lose their distinct identity or autonomy." That's the most interesting part for me. The products offered by hidden champions go unnoticed by consumers. Such businesses not only go unnoticed by consumers, I think they also go unnoticed by investors. A related tendency of the market is to categorize all businesses in a commodity industry as crappy businesses, something that I referred to in the context of the airline industry just now. Indeed, some of the best ideas in which my colleagues and I have invested have exploited these prejudices of Mr. Market-- mispriced B-to-B businesses which have business models as good or even better than some exceptional B-to-C businesses as well as profitable niches hiding inside commodity industries. Indeed, Buffett and Munger love the idea of investing in profitable niche businesses operating in industries with commodity characteristics. For example, Berkshire owns several profitable niche insurance operations. And I quote, "The insurance industry is cursed with a set of dismal economic characteristics that make for a poor long-term outlook-- hundreds of competitors, ease of entry, and product that cannot be differentiated in any meaningful way. In such a commodity-like business, only the low cost operator or someone operating in a protected, usually small niche can sustain high profitability levels." Charlie Munger has said that, "in nature and in business, specialization is key. Just as in an ecosystem, people who narrowly specialize can get terribly good at occupying some little niche, just as animals flourish in niches, similarly, people who specialize in the business world-- and get very good because they specialze-- frequently find good economics that they wouldn't find in any other way." So I think it makes a lot of sense for investors to look for profitable niches in commodity industries which are priced and-- mispriced, rather-- as commodity businesses. That's the categorization that the market is applying to them. That's the label that the market is applying to them, painting everything with the same brush, throwing the baby out with the bath water. The third prejudice that I have is called learning machines. Now you live in a world-- you live in that part of the world-- where making mistakes and encountering failures is celebrated and is often a precondition for getting funding from VCs or even a job. The world out there is actually quite different from all of this. Where I come from, Mr. Market has a prejudice against people who make mistakes. For a while, it is unable to distinguish between people who make mistakes and will continue to make them and people who Charlie Munger would call learning machines. In other words, it has a tendency of categorizing all mistaken entrepreneurs as dumb people. This prejudice doesn't last forever, of course. But sometimes it lasts long enough to make it exploitable. A few years ago, I invested in a business which, at one time, was in bankruptcy but is, today, one of India's most profitable listed businesses as measured by return on invested capital. The chief cause of bankruptcy was a series of mistakes made by its founder. Unlike many other entrepreneurs however, this entrepreneur was not only candid about his mistakes, he was also determined not to make them again. And he didn't. He got rid of a lot of business that destroyed value and became really good at doing one thing really well. He outsourced manufacturing operations to eight vendors, which dramatically boosted returns on capital. He got out of debt and has a liquid balance sheet with surplus cash and has committed that he will never borrow money again. He made a very wise acquisition at a ridiculously low price which not only gave him access to important patented technology, it also opened up a new big market for him. And there was this period of time when the market pretty much ignored all the lessons he had learned. And the stock continued to languish even though, during that time, his company became the world's most dominant player in that industry. But as Graham says, in the long run, the market is a weighing machine. And that's how I treated this business too. Today, it is far more appropriately valued and it's obvious that Mr. Market has overcome its prejudice against this particular learning machine. There's a pattern here, of course. I think value investors should consciously look for learning machines which haven't been forgiven for their past mistakes. That's a prejudice worth exploiting. The fourth one-- I have five in total-- is called serial acquirers. It's a well-known fact that most acquisitions don't create value. That's because the acquirers become overly optimistic about the prospects of targets and overestimate the synergies of acquisitions. So we know the baseline information for acquisition really sucks. So statistically speaking, the stock market is absolutely right to view serial acquirers with a great deal of skepticism. But this doesn't have to mean that all serial acquirers will destroy value. There are a few exceptions. And sometimes the market is prejudiced against them. The market's tendency to categorize all serial acquirers as value destroyers is an exploitable prejudice in my view. There are examples. Let's look at the common factors in these serial acquirers which do create value. There a few examples. Henry Singleton was one. Warren Buffett clearly is one. [INAUDIBLE] financial is another one. The common factors, in my view, are, one, extreme financial discipline-- that is, willingness to walk away from a deal that doesn't make economic sense-- two, providing a permanent home to a promising business, which is something private equity funds cannot do, three, preserving the successful culture of the acquired business, and four, providing growth capital for sensible inorganic growth through bolt-on acquisitions. For value investors, making an investment in such a business when the market is prejudiced against it makes a lot of economic sense because of the option value embedded in such a situation. Successful serial acquirers like Berkshire have carved out a niche for themselves to become preferred owners of wonderful businesses. This competitive advantage of sourcing deals not available to others has significant option value over time. The investor is, in effect, to borrow a term coined by Professor Richard Zeckhouser in his wonderful paper titled "investing in the Unknown and the Unknowable," a sidecar investment, which is an individual who has exceptional sourcing skills and a track record of value creation through inorganic growth. The investor rides around in a sidecar pulled by a powerful motorcycle. The more the investor is distinctively positioned to have confidence in the driver's integrity and his motorcycle's capabilities, the more attractive the investment. Prejudice five is called freaks and misfits. Now I'm almost sure you've seen this before. A few months ago, someone asked a question on Quora. The question is on the screen. And Elon Musk's ex-wife, Justine, gave an answer which went viral and ended up being quoted by "New York Times," "Vox," CNBC, CNN, "The Huffington Post," and "Time" magazine. Here's an excerpt from her reply. "Extreme success results from extreme personality and comes at the cost of many other things. Extreme success is different from what I suppose you would call success. So know that you don't have to be Richard or Elon to be affluent and accomplished and maintain a great lifestyle. Your odds of happiness are better that way." "But if you are extreme, you must be what you are, which means that happiness is more or less besides the point. These people tend to be freaks and misfits who are forced to experience the world in an unusually challenging way. They develop strategies to survive. And as they grew older, they found ways to apply these strategies to other things and create for themselves a distinct and power advantage." "They don't think the way other people think. They see things from angles that unlock new ideas and insights. Other people consider them to be somewhat insane." The term "freaks and misfits," which might ring a bell with you given the culture that we are in, was taken from Justine. I think it's important for us to understand her perspective. And that is something that a professor from Harvard Business School, Joseph Badaracco, offers an explanation. Here the professor uses literary fiction to teach leadership to the students at Harvard Business School. In this book "Questions of Character" he writes, "How does serious fiction help us understand leadership? The answer is simple but extraordinarily powerful. Serious fiction gives us a unique inside view of leadership. In real life, most people see the leaders of their organizations only occasionally"-- as investors, this is exactly what we get to see. We don't get to see what is really happening-- "and only get a fleeting glimpse of what these leaders are thinking and feeling." "Even interviews with executives have limits. Executives only say so much. And even when they want to be candid, sensitivities have to be observed, memory fades and sometimes distorts, and success crowds out failures. In contrast, serious literature offers a view from the inside. It opens doors to a world rarely seen except, on occasion, by leaders' spouses and closest friends." Think Justine Musk. "It lets us watch leaders as they think, work, hope, hesitate, commit, exalt, regret, and reflect. We see their characters tested, reshaped, strengthened, or weakened." The reason why Justine's perspective is important for us is because, as the professor puts it, "it opens doors to a world rarely seen, except, on occasion, by leaders' spouses and closest friends." In my view, when it comes to evaluating the quality of extremely successful entrepreneurs in the early part of the journey, the market displays a prejudice. This prejudice is derived not only from the complex personality that some of these entrepreneurs have, many of the whom are definitely not likable people, but also from a limited view about the individual in question that investors get. I've seen this prejudice play out over and over again. The market is just too judgmental about some of them. [VIDEO PLAYBACK] [CAR HORN] [DOG BARKING] -Look at the cute dog. [DOG BARKING] -All the boys are calling, crazy girl. -I hope she sings this tonight. -I know. -Hey dad, pull over. We need gum. -I'm on it. Oh, honey, here's some money. -What do we get here? [POLICE SIREN] -Hello. [END PLAYBACK] SANJAY BAKSHI: I see this play out over and over again in analyzing these human beings, extraordinary human beings. The reality is that the riding on the coat tails of such extraordinary human beings is a key source of compounding capital for public market investors. Charlie agrees. In an interview with Miguel Barbosa of Simoleon Sense, successful value investor Paul Lountzis has said, "The ability to identify a young Phil Knight, a young Howard Shultz from Starbucks, a young John Mackey from Whole Foods is becoming increasingly important." I'm typically attracted to a company because of the numbers. But what makes you enormously successful for your clients is when you identify qualitative factors that are yet to appear in the quantitative results. The key is to identify these situations early. You still have those opportunities when companies are small, but it's getting harder because there are many smart people looking. For example, if you see Progressive Insurance generating an 82 combined ratio and making $0.18 on every dollar on their underwriting before investment income, you might say, my god, State Farm is at 110. How are these guys so profitable? It's really hard to identify these unique teams and cultures. But if you can do it or get lucky, then you can do very well for your clients. By having an edge, you will avoid overpaying. You're protected on the downside and you have enormous upside because you're piggybacking on a visionary who's building an extraordinary culture. With the long-run way, because of this mispricing, you can stay with them for 20 years. Furthermore, because you have done your research, and you understand how this visionary is building the business, and you have the confidence to survive all the vicissitudes of the market, when you go through tough times, you recognize they have a stable competitive advantage. They've got better people, they're tenacious, and they're likely to come out stronger. It's an important distinction that I'm trying to make that the qualitative is becoming more important. I still think quantitative features are subordinate to the business model in valuation, but the business model is infinity more impacted by management and culture than it was in the past. I think it's terribly important for value investors to recognize that a key source of investment success is to become long-term passive partners with extraordinary human beings who many would regard as freaks or misfits. When George Bernard Shaw said that "the reasonable man adapts himself to the world; the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself. Therefore all progress depends on the unreasonable man," was he talking about freaks and misfits? Shouldn't the label of freak and misfit not sometimes be relabeled as intelligent fanatics? That's what this bias is about, the representativeness heuristic, labels. We apply labels. And a label of a freak and misfit, which is a negative connotation, can easily be sometimes relabeled as an intelligent fanatic. And it makes all the difference. One of my key learnings from studying such people is that, as an investor, I have to teach myself to overlook many of their personality traits, some of which are not admirable at all. Indeed, I think those traits are a consequence of their fanatic focus on their work. I have been consciously training myself to empathize with such extraordinary human beings. In his wonderful book "The Social Animal," Elliot Aronson talks about the insidious nature of prejudice. He quotes a fictional dialogue from Gordon Allport's classic book "The Nature of Prejudice." I think the dialogue is worth reading. Mr. X says that "the trouble with Jews is that they only take care of their own group." Mr. Y, who's the prejudiced person, says-- sorry, Mr. X is the prejudiced person. Mr. Y is the interrogator. He says, "But the record of the Community Chest campaign shows that they give more generously, in proportion to their numbers, to the general charities of the community than do non-Jews." Mr. X then responds, "That shows they're always trying to buy favor and intrude into Christian affairs. They think of nothing but money. And that's why there are so many Jewish bankers." Mr. Y responds, "But a recent study shows that the percentage of Jews in the banking business is negligible, far smaller than the percentage of non-Jews." Mr. X then responds, "That's just it. They don't go in for respectable businesses. They're only in the movie business or they run nightclubs." The dialogue illustrates the insidious nature of prejudice far better than the mountain of definitions. In effect, the prejudiced Mr. X is saying, don't trouble me with the facts. My mind is made up. He makes no attempt to dispute the data presented by Mr. Y. He either distorts the facts in order to make them support his hatred of Jews or he bounces off them, undaunted, to a new area of attack. A deeply prejudiced person is virtually immune to information at variance with his or her cherished stereotypes. As famed jurist Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. once said, "Trying to educate a bigot is like shining light into the pupil of an eye-- it constricts." Whlie Aronson's words, that a deeply prejudiced person is virtually immune to information at variance with his or her cherished stereotypes, apply to many prejudiced human beings, they do apply, if you think about it, to Mr. Market. That's because Mr. Market is a learning machine. He corrects his prejudices over time. While the five patterns of prejudice that I just outlined they keep coming back in one form or the other, the prejudice against specific examples conforming to these patterns tends to disappear over time. We have a name for that, and we call that rerating. I think there are two lessons here. The first one I've already told you about. The second one is that we should look at Mr. Market with some respect. After all, he's far less prejudiced than us. Why couldn't we learn to get rid of some of our own prejudices from him. Thank you. [APPLAUSE] MALE SPEAKER: Thank you, Sanjay. This was great. So we'll open up to some questions right now. AUDIENCE: Thank you, Sanjay, for the wonderful presentation. I had a question about the last one, misfits, and maybe a little bit about the learning machines. If we take Warren Buffett as an example, you could say, ignoring the past decade, most of the investments he's made are in a handful of companies, Geico, American Express in the beginning, in the '60s, American Express again in the '90s, and a few handful of others. Almost all of them he bought at points of maximum pessimism. I can't maybe recollect any example where he said, everything is great with the business. And here's a misfit. Here's a learning machine. And I'm going to buy it. I think Coke may be one such example. But there are more examples where it was essentially, he was focused on the long term, there was something temporarily wrong with the business, and he bought it. He talks about jumping one-foot hurdles. Sounds to me this is more than a one-foot hurdle, identifying a misfit or a learning machine. But maybe I don't know any examples. Maybe you can enlighten us. SANJAY BAKSHI: Sure. I think it's important to recognize that the examples that you cited refer to what he's done in public markets. And what he does in public markets actually is a very small portion of what actually really happens in Berkshire. As you probably know, they have, I think, more than 80 businesses now, in their portfolio, which they own wholly or almost wholly. And they have been generating a lot of cash. So there have been all these businesses. When I talked about the idea of misfits, I was really referring to the apprehensions that public market investors have about the character of these people. Sometimes these people do things which look very, very odd. And they odd in the since that, after all, these are extraordinary human beings. They don't do things which look ordinary. And I'm not talking about innovation. Of course that is one aspect. I'm not talking about risk taking, or innovation, or any of that. I'm talking about things that appear to be sometimes unethical, but they really are not a big deal in the whole totality of things. So I'll give an example without naming names. There are businesses which I have looked at in the past where the entrepreneur may have paid himself a really nice salary. Now if you focus only on that aspect-- and it may turn out to be something like 10% of profits. But the fact of the matter is that he's an extraordinary human being. And 10% does look big. But if you look at the overall situation-- if you look at the fact of what he's accomplished and the kind of moat that he has built-- in the totality of things, you just suck up. And you have a choice. Either you want to be a partner with him or not. But I think the opportunity cost of not being a partner with a guy like him, an extraordinary person, is actually quite high. So you have to swallow a lot of things which may, under normal circumstances, be something that you might want to walk away from. And the reason is because of the extraordinary moat that he has created. So that's just one example. I'll give you a few other examples. I know of a business where the premier credit rating company in the country resigned the assignment. Why? Because he's not cooperating. He basically told them, buzz off. I'm not going to give you the information. And if you remember, Charlie Munger did pretty much the same thing with the auditors in "Daily Journal." And he had a huge tiff with the auditors. That's the point I'm making. These guys have what Charlie Munger called a lot of chutzpah. They absolutely don't give a shit about what anybody else thinks about them. They think they're absolutely right. And it reminds me of what Charlie Munger has said, never underestimate a man who overestimates himself. And all entrepreneurs overestimate themselves. And overconfidence is a very important aspect of capitalism. What I'm trying to distinguish is between the dumb fanatics and the intelligent fanatics. And I gave a talk sometime back when I made that distinction where I profiled seven intelligent fanatics from India. And I gave a kind of a checklist as to how I think about intelligent fanatics versus dumb fanatics. So one of them is debt or risk management. So a dumb fanatic would-- they're all overconfident whether you're dumb or not. But they bet the bank. And sometimes they get lucky. Most of the time, they blow up. So they don't know anything about risk management. Whereas an intelligent fanatic would make a series of bets. He's, like, writing insurance. And many of those bets will fail. But even if all of them fail, that doesn't destroy the company. So that's one. The other is they almost certainly don't rely on other people's money. They use their own capital. They don't borrow money. So they don't create financial structures where they are dependent upon the kindness of strangers over there. So I see that. I see fanaticism, when combined with intelligence, that combined together, makes a very nice combination. You see that it's so rare. If you look at the history of wealth creation, when you find this fanaticism with intelligence and integrity-- when you combine those three-- and if you can get it along with a reasonable business-- and that's the point I'm making here, which is the point that even in commodity industries, some entrepreneurs have the ability to carve out a niche which is very hard to copy. And that niche is coming from the fanaticism of the entrepreneur. As it's a very smart person. And therefore, if you can become partners with him on favorable terms in terms of valuation and all of that, then you can ignore a lot of other things, which is what Elon Musk's ex-wife was saying. They are crazy in many ways. These guys-- or women-- they are very nutty in many ways. But I think you should not over-focus on those matters. You should only focus on the track record-- what they do, how they run their business operations. MALE SPEAKER: So if I can just push that question a little bit further-- SANJAY BAKSHI: Yes, Soreb. MALE SPEAKER: So not to say that there are no intelligent fanatics and so on, but to borrow that phrase of whether it is actually a one-foot hurdle versus a six-foot hurdle, so to say-- SANJAY BAKSHI: It doesn't have to be. You see, the point is if you're going to-- what are we trying to do here? We're trying to compound capital, right? We are doing it sitting in our offices in an air-conditioned environment without stepping out or actually [INAUDIBLE] try to become rich. So it shouldn't be easy. I don't think the idea of compounding capital at superlative rates of return over long periods of time should become extraordinarily easy for anybody. If it was, then those returns will go away. So I don't think it should be that easy. When Mr. Buffett talks about one-foot hurdles, he's talking about his ability to predict the fundamental economics of a business over a long period of time. And believe it or not, many businesses that he has invested in are actually quite complex. So for a lot of people, the ability to understand supercar insurance is actually very, very different. But he has done that. So he defines a circle of competence and he tries to stay within that circle of competence. And I think that's a wonderful model to have. But to assume that you will find very simple things to do all along, I think that's something which I don't really believe in. AUDIENCE: I have a two-part question. Why is it that the stereotyping-- is it correct or incorrect-- is often found in hindsight, with the benefit of hindsight. With the disparities that you listed, all five of them, are there certain tips or shortcuts, further shortcuts, which you can tell to distinguish between what could be an incorrect assessment of opportunities which the market could correlate over time? Like, how would you distinguish between luck and skill and define this? SANJAY BAKSHI: Track record. Track record. You're really looking at the long-term track record. If it was all luck, then over a period of time, that would go away, right? What I'm trying to illustrate is the point that there are these patterns that play out. What we're trying to do is if we picked one-- I picked this one heuristic, the representative. There are many others. I just picked one and I tried to think about the various manifestations in which it occurs, which creates tradable opportunities for public market investors. What I found was that the whole idea of labeling-- and I mentioned that some time ago, that intelligent fanatic is just a label. To somebody else, it might look like a freak person. But to somebody else, it could be an intelligent fanatic. But what is the truth? The truth lies in the numbers. The truth lies in what they actually accomplish. So what we're really looking at is, for example, in an industry with sub-normal profitability-- take airlines. We saw that-- there is one company which has extraordinary profitability. So we all question why, why is that happening. Is this luck or is this skill? And to answer that, you have to look at the record over a long period of time. You have to look at the track record of that business during periods when the airline industry was going through a horrible period of time. And if you do that for Ryanair and for Southwest, you will find that they had some unusual fundamental financial performance even during periods when the entire airline industry in the world was going through a terrible phase. So you try to look for exceptional, outstanding performance over long periods of time. And then you attribute that to luck or skill. And occasionally, you will find that there is some skill out there. The beauty is that the market is not able to distinguish that. The market has this labeling problem. The market thinks, oh, it's a crappy business because it's in the airline industry and because Warren Buffett says so. Therefore it should not be priced as a real good quality business. But if we ignore for the moment, if you de-bias yourself, if you remove the name, the label of the airline industry and think like a Graham, who said, once, I want to be completely unbiased. I don't want to even know the name of the business, if you just look at the actual objective data, you will find staggering financial performance. You won't know what the industry is. Just because you know that the industry is an airline industry and there is this label hovering around in your head that airlines are, generally speaking-- and that's a correct label-- crappy businesses, you tend to misjudge what you are seeing. And I think that's a bias that is worth getting out of, because that's an exploitable bias. That's a bias that the market will, itself, get out of, which is where the opportunity lies. Because you are trying to buy it when the market still has that bias. And when the market doesn't, the stock would have been rerated and you would have made a lot of money. You see, the whole idea in my work in investing in modern businesses, what I found was the idea that moats can only be found in some industries and never in other industries, that itself is a prejudice. If you work hard enough, even in businesses which have commodity labels, you will find moated businesses, usually in niches. And when you find them, you may often find that the market is still treating them as a commodity business. That's the opportunity. AUDIENCE: So you spoke about many value investors shying away from buying 25x multiples and higher than that. And I think you also spoke about intelligent fanatics and people who are driven and obsessed by growth and returning profits. I guess the question I have is, where does a healthy margin of safety come into all of this. I think one of the reasons I shy away from a 25x multiple is, what's my margin of safety, right. I look at the previous pace it's been trading at. I look at its growth. When I'm buying something at a P/E value of 25, I'm expecting 10%, 15% growth year-on-year for the next decade, right? So I just wanted to hear your thoughts on that. SANJAY BAKSHI: Sure. I'll answer that in two parts. Firstly, when you think about P/E multiple, the P part is obvious because it's observed from the market. It's the E part which is quite subjective. And I mentioned this-- in my judgment, in many moated businesses, the E part is higher than what you see over there for reasons that I explained. And when you make those adjustments, then what looks expensive is not that expensive. It's cheaper. That's one. Secondly, if you look at a business that generally has a moat-- that means it has strong entry barriers and it has the ability to compound capital at lucrative rates for long periods of time-- if you do the math, as Charlie has mentioned, even if you pay a 25 P/E multiple for a business which is compounding capital internally at a fabulous rate and has reinvestment opportunities, it's the duration of the opportunity. If you extend that from five years to 10 years, and from 10 to a longer period if you have that conviction, then it becomes quite attractive. I think you may be referring to some businesses in this part of the word where the growth rates are actually lower. Where I come from, growth rates in many business are actually very high. They are sometimes in high double-digit percentage numbers. AUDIENCE: In the context of investing in Asian countries, two things that come up and which cloud every other kind of judgment for right or wrong is the authenticity of what you see on the books. So first of all, a company could be doing well for 10 years, 20 years. And these are very, very big numbers. Some company is doing good for two decades. And eventually something blows up. And what you figure out is that was a very, very big fraud going on. It could be numbers, could be because the auditors were being bribed and all those things. It happens more in Asian countries than, probably, North America. SANJAY BAKSHI: Is that a prejudice? AUDIENCE: Could be. But when you're identifying an individual company and you see returns which far surpass the returns of other companies in the same industry, one thing that one also needs to scrutinize is, is there some kind of a fraud that's going on over there. SANJAY BAKSHI: Absolutely. That's the whole point of being an analyst is that you have to be skeptical. You have to have the diligence. You have to be able to check the numbers. You have to do background checks. There are a lot of things that you need to do to make sure that the numbers are right. If the numbers are not right, then obviously you shouldn't be investing in that anyway. Because if they can cook the books, then you really don't want to be a partner in a business run by a person who is cooking the books, right? So I think it's absolutely imperative that you do that test. And it doesn't matter which country you are in. I think that there was a Madoff here and there was an Enron here as well. So it's something that is a required discipline for any value investor, to be able to do ascertain whether the numbers are cooked or not. AUDIENCE: So how to do that in-- SANJAY BAKSHI: I can do a whole course on that. AUDIENCE: OK. SANJAY BAKSHI: Yeah, but we can talk after this. There are some things. It depends on the industry. If you have to do that in the banking industry it becomes far more complex. It's a very different kind of business model. If you're looking at a simpler business model then there are ways of doing that. And I'll be happy to talk to you after about this. MALE SPEAKER: So because this was a central point in, at least, the last half of your talk, some of us were at the "Daily Journal" meeting where Charlie Munger was asked a question about Elon Musk. So I have a couple of the sentences from Bloomberg Business's website. And Charlie says, "I think Elon Musk is a genius, and I don't use that word lightly. He's also one of the boldest men who ever came down the pike. So put me down as saying I've always been afraid of the guy whose IQ is 190 and he thinks it's 250." So like you said, never underestimate a person who is overconfident. But I think identifying intelligent fanatics, so to say, versus investing in Tesla or [INAUDIBLE], aren't they two separate questions? SANJAY BAKSHI: They are very different questions. All I'm looking at is, without giving up on Buffett kind of thinking, without giving up on the idea of investing in highly profitable, dominant businesses which are already making a lot of money and paying reasonable multiples of their earning power, particularly when they're run by an intelligent fanatic, is a great combination. I'm not recommending Tesla, nor am I recommending Amazon.com or any of the businesses that you might relate to the idea of intelligent fanatics. I'm just saying, because you can easily relate to those human beings, that there are these people out there. They're not as well known as these human beings are. But there are these people out there. They are achieving global dominance. And it's just a label. The point I'm trying to make is that this whole talk was aboard labels, labels as prejudices. And therefore, sometimes a prejudice which is labeled as a freak or a misfit, actually, the correct label to apply to that is that of an intelligent fanatic. And it doesn't have to be an Elon Musk. It doesn't have to be a Jeff Bezos or anybody for that matter. It has to be somebody who's really passionate, has got integrity, is completing driven, is not dumb in the sense that it will not blow up the balance sheet on a single idea, it will not lever up the balance sheet. It's conservative and aggressive in a combination that is reflective of intelligence. And if you can find that combination along with a great business or even a reasonable business, that's the point of making. You don't have to look for the best quality businesses out there because they get priced out. In a parimutual system of the stock market, you can't bet on the best horses. Because the best horses, the odds change. You are betting against other investors. And therefore, what you should really be trying to do is find reasonable quality businesses which have the taint of a commodity on them, but the particular business that you are looking at is an exception. It's an exception because it's run by a fellow or a bunch of people who are really exceptional. And you have got data to validate that. You're not just dreaming it up. You're not just seeing it because you read a prospectus on an IPO, and you think that he will do wonderful things, and you believe he'll do wonderful things. You actually have seen that information. You've seen that they have actually delivered, under terrible conditions, fundamental performance which is outstanding in relation to their peers in the industry. And you think that you can attribute that to certain causal factors that you can identify. And those factors will remain for a long, long time. If you can find that with a reasonable valuation, even in a normal industry-- not an extraordinary profitable industry where everybody makes money-- I think it's a wonderful combination, because the market is mispricing it. MALE SPEAKER: Great. So thank you, Sanjay, for a fantastic talk. It was a pleasure to have you here. SANJAY BAKSHI: Thank you. Thank you for having me. [APPLAUSE]
